title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's digest across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Each section leads with the practical takeaway and flags how strong the evidence is (RCT vs. review vs. preclinical). Citations are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — talk to a clinician before acting on anything here.

sections.body:
This week's theme: among the popular "longevity" supplements, **urolithin A** still has the most coherent human evidence, while **rapamycin** and **senolytics** remain promising but unproven for healthy aging.

- **Urolithin A leads the pack.** A 2026 comparative review of urolithin A, spermidine, and NAD+ precursors concluded UA has the best-aligned mechanistic, biomarker, and early functional evidence — especially for **mitochondrial health, muscle endurance, and immune aging**. A 2025 *Nature Aging* RCT (50 adults, 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks) showed UA shifted CD8+ T cells toward a younger, less-exhausted profile. An **NIH/NIA trial** of UA on glucose metabolism in adults 55+ begins recruiting **Nov 25**.
- **Rapamycin: safe, but no clear anti-aging win.** The 2025 **PEARL** trial (intermittent low-dose rapamycin, 48 weeks) was reasonably safe with only **modest** secondary gains (muscle mass, pain in women) and **no** improvement on predefined aging endpoints.
- **NAD+ & senolytics.** NR/NMN reliably raise NAD+ biomarkers but show inconsistent clinical benefit. Senolytics (dasatinib+quercetin) improved bone density only in women with the highest senescent-cell burden — still early.

Takeaway: expect **modest** effects, favor compounds with human RCTs, and be skeptical of single-supplement longevity claims.

sources.title: Urolithin A, Spermidine, and NAD+ Precursors in Human Healthy Aging: A Comparative Narrative Review of Recent Clinical Evidence
Effect of the mitophagy inducer urolithin A on age-related immune decline: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial
Geroprotective Effects of Drugs Modulating Metabolic Pathways (PEARL rapamycin trial; senolytics)
Effects of Urolithin A Supplementation on Glucose Metabolism in Healthy Adults 55+ (recruiting; starts Nov 25 2026)

sections.body:
The 2026 message is consistent: HIIT is a **time-efficient way to boost cardio fitness**, but it works best **paired with strength training**.

- **Older & middle-aged women.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* meta-analysis (19 RCTs) found HIIT produced a **large, high-certainty improvement in VO2max** (SMD 1.20) — but **no significant gain in muscle strength** and only borderline walking-ability benefit. The authors' conclusion: HIIT alone is *insufficient* to fully improve functional performance.
- **Overweight/obese women.** A second 2026 meta-analysis (15 RCTs) found HIIT significantly **lowered body weight, BMI, body-fat %, and fat mass** and raised VO2max, with favorable HDL/LDL shifts. Effects on total cholesterol and triglycerides were uncertain.
- **Postmenopausal heart health.** A 2026 network meta-analysis ranked HIIT highest for lowering **triglycerides**, though that estimate rested on only three studies — treat it as suggestive, not settled.

Takeaway: intensity drives the cardio and body-composition wins; **add resistance work**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sources.title: Effects of HIIT on cardiopulmonary fitness and physical function in middle-aged and elderly women: systematic review & meta-analysis
Effects of HIIT on body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness, and lipids in adult women with overweight or obesity: systematic review & meta-analysis
Exercise dose and triglyceride reduction in postmenopausal women: systematic review & network meta-analysis

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). New 2026 trials sharpen two practical points: *how* you train matters, and *add-ons* can help tougher cases.

- **PFMT beats Pilates.** A 2026 RCT (105 women, 6 weeks) found targeted PFMT reduced incontinence impact far more than Pilates — with or without pelvic-floor cueing (ICIQ-SF dropped **−4.4** for PFMT vs. −0.7 for Pilates) — and produced bigger gains in muscle strength and squeeze pressure. Dedicated pelvic-floor work outperforms general core exercise.
- **Supervised beats unsupervised.** A 2026 RCT found **supervised** PFMT cut pad-test leakage dramatically (22.9 g → 3.2 g) while home-only training barely moved — though unsupervised remains a reasonable option when adherence is good.
- **Very weak muscles? Add stimulation.** A 2026 double-blind trial showed adding sEMG-triggered electrical stimulation to supervised PFMT gave extra, durable strength gains (sustained at 12 months) in women with very weak pelvic floors.

Takeaway: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps** — confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback.

sources.title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training Outperforms Pilates in Women with Stress Urinary Incontinence: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Managing Female SUI: A Randomized Control Trial Evaluating Supervised vs. Unsupervised Pelvic Floor Muscle Training
Pelvic muscle training and electrostimulation to treat weak pelvic floor: a multicentre randomised parallel-group trial

sections.topic: Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
Read "alternative" as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard HER2-targeted therapy** — never a replacement. Two 2026 themes stand out.

- **Correct vitamin D deficiency.** A 2026 *Nutrients* retrospective study of curative-intent HER2+ patients found that *failing* to correct a deficiency carried a **~1.7× higher recurrence risk**, with a dose-response trend (best outcomes at D25 >50 ng/mL). Two 2025 RCTs reported a **doubling of pathologic complete response** with repletion, strongest in HER2+ and triple-negative disease. Notably, **TP53** ties in here: HER2+ tumors carry TP53 mutations ~55–75% of the time, and in a TP53-mutated subset of the AMATERASU trial, vitamin D sharply improved relapse-free survival — hinting TP53 status may flag who benefits.
- **Supplements: mechanism ahead of proof.** A 2026 systematic review found **omega-3s** during chemo are generally well tolerated but show **no proven** survival or treatment-response benefit (very-low-certainty evidence). A 2026 review of **green-tea/polyphenols** shows p53-pathway activity in the lab, but effects depend on p53 status and **lack clinical validation**.

Takeaway: use integrative options as *add-ons coordinated with your oncology team* — watch for interactions with targeted therapy.

sources.title: Vitamin D Replacement After Deficiency and Disease-Free Survival in Curative-Intent HER2+ Breast Cancer (TP53/VDR cross-talk; AMATERASU subset)
DHA / EPA+DHA (±GLA, ±Vitamin D) During Chemotherapy in Women with Breast Cancer: An Intervention- and Outcome-Stratified Systematic Review
Polyphenol-based interventions in breast cancer: signaling pathways, p53 modulation, and translational strategies (Review)

sections.body:
For restless or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I is first-line.** A 2026 *Nature Reviews Disease Primers* overview reaffirms **cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)** as first-line, with **digital CBT-I** offering a scalable, at-home option. It targets exactly the problems you care about — trouble falling asleep, waking in the night, and fragmented sleep.
- **Habits help, but aren't enough alone.** A 2026 multi-society position statement stresses that **sleep hygiene by itself is not adequate** for chronic insomnia — it supports CBT-I rather than replacing it. Medications are second-line and short-term: z-drugs/benzodiazepines for **2–4 weeks**, melatonin up to ~13 weeks, orexin antagonists for chronic use.
- **Supplements, honestly.** A 2026 review of 12 RCTs found **magnesium is not a reliable insomnia treatment** (low-certainty, mixed results; at most a small subjective benefit). **Melatonin** evidence more often favors placebo-beating effects, but mainly for **falling asleep faster / circadian issues** — not for staying asleep.

Best-practice habits: **fixed wake time** daily; bed for sleep only; cool, dark, quiet room; dim lights and screens before bed; and see a provider if disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks (to rule out sleep apnea).

sources.title: Management of adult insomnia in Australia: a joint position statement (sleep hygiene inadequate alone; CBT-I first-line; medication guidance)
Magnesium Supplementation for Sleep in Adults: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
Exogenous Melatonin and Sleep Quality: A Scoping Review of Systematic Reviews
